E15.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being burned.

E15.2.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 340 n. 225, 350 n. 260, (Modoc): Curtin Myths of the Modocs (Boston, 1912) 31.
E15.2.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being made to sweat.

E15.3.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being stewed.

E16.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being stung, the corpse being laid on an ant-heap.

E17.p: A dead person is brought back to life when someone or something licks the corpse.

E17.1.p: A dead person bitten by a snake is revived when the snake licks the bite it made.

E18.r: N. A. Indian (Tlingit): Golder JAFL XX 292.
E18.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being tickled.

E21.1.p: A poisoned person is revived when the poisoned apple lodged in their throat is shaken or dislodged.

E21.1.1.p: A dead man is revived when the poisoned cobra flesh is removed from his mouth.

E21.2.p: A girl who has fainted from being laced too tightly in a corset is revived when the lace that is strangling her breaks, and her brothers carry her to the grave.

E21.3.p: A poisoned person is revived when the poisoned comb is removed from their head or hair.

E21.4.r: Africa (Tonga): Junod 266ff., (Swahili): Baker FL XXXVIII 299ff. No. 16.
E21.4.p: A poisoned person is revived when the poisoned slippers are removed from their feet.

E21.5.p: A poisoned person is revived when someone sucks the poison out of the wound.

E23.p: A dead person is brought back to life when caught in a snare.

E25.r: Frequently combined with E61. N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 319 n. 153. See also references to E61.
E25.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being frightened.

E26.r: Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 1; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 88.
E26.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being shouted at.

E26.1.p: A dead person is brought back to life when someone commands them to arise.

E27.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being slung or thrown against something.

E29.p: A dead person is brought back to life by rough treatment not covered by the other headings in this group.

E29.1.p: A dead person is brought back to life by having their bone bitten.

E29.3.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 57, 81.
E29.3.p: A dead person is brought back to life by pricking their anus.

E29.4.p: A dead person, whose soul is held in a flower, is brought back to life by plucking that flower.

E29.4.1.p: A dead person, whose soul is held in a tree, is brought back to life by felling the tree and splitting its trunk in two.

E29.5.p: A dead person whose soul is held in birds is brought back to life by cutting off the birds' heads.

E29.6.p: A dead person is brought back to life by having urine poured on one of their bones.

E29.7.p: A dead person is brought back to life by being struck by lightning.

E341.2.p: A dead person returns to thank someone for giving them food.

E341.3.p: A dead person returns to thank someone for saying prayers on their behalf.

E341.4.p: A dead person returns to thank someone for giving them clothing, specifically a shirt.

E341.5.p: A priest who has died comes back to save a gambler from the devil, repaying an earlier favor.

E342.p: A dead person returns to carry out a bargain they made while alive.

E345.p: A dead person returns to make right an injury or wrong they did while alive.

E345.1.p: A dead person returns to put back the boundary markers they had moved or removed.

E351.r: Herbert III 96 No. 38; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 327 No. 23; cf. French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 13; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 53, 97, Beal XXI 319, 331; Scotland: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
E351.p: A dead person returns to pay back a money debt they owed while alive.

E352.r: *BP III 235; Tobler 65; Fb “gjenganger” I 443b.—Irish: O’Suilleabhain 98, Beal XXI 331; England: *Baughman; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 313 No. 80, 327 No. 23.
E352.p: A dead person returns to give back goods they had stolen while alive.

E353.p: A dead man asks that a girl he seduced while alive be married to him, so that he can make amends.

E360.p: Other reasons, not covered by the more specific headings, why a dead person comes back in a friendly way.

E361.r: *BP II 485; Wimberly 110, 230ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 433a s.v. “Eddamärchen”; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 831; Legenda Aurea (ed. E361.p: A dead person returns to get the living to stop weeping over them.

E361.1.r: N. A. Indian (Thompson River): Alexander N. Am. 137.
E361.1.p: A tear shed by a living person in the world of the living falls on the dead in the underworld, and the dead brother sends back a comforting message.

E361.2.p: A dead person returns to bring a consoling message to the living.

E361.3.p: A dead son returns to tell his mother that no mortal can escape death.

E363.p: A ghost returns to help the living in some way.

E363.1.p: A ghost returns to help the living out of a sudden emergency.

E363.1.1.p: A dead woman's ghost takes the place of a living bride on her journey to her wedding. The ghost travels in her stead and fulfills the role.

E363.2.p: A dead person's ghost comes back to guard or shield living people from harm.

E363.3.p: A ghost comes back to warn living people of danger or misfortune.

E363.4.p: A dead person returns to comfort or reassure living people who are worried or afraid.

E363.5.p: A dead person returns and gives material goods or possessions to help the living.

E363.5.1.p: The ghost of a murdered girl lends jewels to a living girl so she can attend a ball, and in return the living girl gives the ghost flowers.

E363.6.p: A ghost helps living people in some other way not covered by the more specific categories.

E364.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3502, Balys Ghosts.
E364.p: A dead person comes back briefly to say goodbye to someone they loved before leaving for good.

E365.r: *Fb “tilgive”, Feilberg DF X 74f; Irish myth: *Cross; Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 115 No. 13.
E365.p: A dead person returns to ask the living for forgiveness for a wrong done in life.

E365.1.p: A dead person returns and grants forgiveness to a living person.

E366.p: A dead person returns to give advice or counsel to a living person.

E366.1.p: A skull that laughs gives advice to a hero.

E366.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3566, Balys Ghosts.
E366.2.p: A hanged man's ghost warns a young man not to visit his sweetheart. The hanged man takes the young man's place and is shot in his stead, receiving the bullet meant for him.

E366.3.p: The bones of a man who was eaten speak and give advice to a hero.

E367.r: Wesselski Arlotto I 201 No. 29; Irish: Beal XXI 332, O’Suilleabhain 100; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 3 No. 23.
E367.p: A dead person returns to urge living people to turn from sin and repent.

E367.1.p: A person who has spent two years in hell comes back and speaks about how important it is to have a religious experience.

E367.2.p: A saint returns from the dead and gives a blessing to the living.

E367.3.p: A dead person returns to foretell the coming of Christ.

E367.4.p: A dead person returns and converts to Christianity.

E367.5.p: A dead woman's ghost scolds a person who does not believe.

E368.r: *Crane Vitry 145f. No. 31; Alphabet Nos. 151, 700; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
E368.p: A dead pupil comes back to tell his former master that studying is pointless.

E371.r: (Cf. E276, E291, E419.11.2.) *Fb “spøgelse” III 521b; Tobler 34f.; Loomis White Magic 53; England, Wales, Ireland, Canada, U.S.: *Baughman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 827.
E371.p: A dead person returns to life or appears as a ghost in order to show where hidden treasure is buried.

E371.1.p: A dead person returns to reveal where stolen goods have been hidden.

E371.2.p: A dead person returns to recite again a long heroic poem he had forgotten or that had been lost.

E371.3.p: A poet keeps singing on the day after his death.

E372.p: A dead person comes back to life or appears as a ghost in order to search for hidden treasure.

E373.p: Ghosts or dead people return and give gifts to the living.

E373.1.r: A voice says: “I am letting it fall.” The man: “Let it.” Money falls to the ground. *Chauvin V 78 No. 22 n. 1; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 123 No. 46; cf. Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 24 No. 216; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3626; India: Thompson-Balys.
E373.1.p: A living person is given money by ghosts as a reward for bravery.

E373.2.p: A living person receives a sword from his dead father, who is summoned up.

E373.3.p: A woman's hand comes up out of her grave and gives a man keeping vigil a letter of salvation.

E373.4.p: A dead person returns to give a tribe the money that a landlord is demanding from them.

E374.p: A dead person comes back to life and tells of a journey to the land of the dead.

E374.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3570.
E374.1.p: A dead friend returns to keep a promise made with another friend, and tells what the land of the dead is like. The two friends had agreed that whichever died first would do so.

E375.p: A dead person returns to stop a thief from escaping.

E376.p: A ghost comes back to confess a wrong it did while alive.

E376.1.p: A saint comes back from the dead to clear a churchman of blame.

E377.p: A dead person comes back to teach the living something.

E377.1.p: A dead poet rises from his grave mound to teach a poem to a herdsman, who then becomes a great poet himself.

E379.p: Miscellaneous motifs of a dead person returning in a friendly way that do not fit the other categories.

E379.1.p: A dead person returns to life or appears as a ghost in order to save someone from drowning.

E379.2.p: A holy hermit's body rises up out of a river to show favor to his disciple.

E379.3.r: S. A. Indian (Guaporé River): Lévy-Strauss III 378.
E379.3.p: A dead person comes back to life or appears again in order to protect friends.

E379.4.p: A ghost works together with a living man as his ally or helper.

E379.5.p: A dead person comes back so that enough men are present to perform a required ritual.

E380.r: *Fb “mane” II 547a; Irish: Beal XXI 310; Scotland: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3513; Jewish: *Neuman; Icelandic: *Boberg.
E380.p: A ghost is called up or brought back from the dead by someone.

E380.1.p: People who summon souls are punished: at the hour of a man's death, the souls overwhelm him.

E381.r: See all references to E361. *Jellinek Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 323f; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 281 n. 41.
E381.p: A ghost is summoned by someone weeping.

E382.p: A ghost is summoned by pouring the blood of sacrifices into a trench.

E383.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 32; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 138 No. 107; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 48 No. 107; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 597, 601; Korean: Zong in-Sob 205.
E383.p: Ghosts are summoned by reading from a sacred book.

E384.p: A ghost is summoned by music.

E384.1.p: A ghost is summoned by beating a drum.

E384.2.p: A ghost is accidentally raised by whistling.

E384.3.r: Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 29; S. A. Indian (Brazil): Oberg 110.
E384.3.p: A ghost is summoned by a blast on a horn (or whistle).

E385.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 99.
E385.p: A husband keeps vigil at his dead wife's grave and so calls her spirit forth.

E385.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 99.
E385.1.p: The ghost of the wife ignores or discourages her husband, who has summoned her.

E386.p: A ghost is summoned by some other means not covered by the more specific categories.

E386.1.p: A ghost is summoned by sprinkling or using holy water.

E386.2.r: Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 98; MacCulloch Eddic 298—300, 312.
E386.2.p: A ghost is summoned by a charm or magic spell.

E386.3.p: Ghosts are summoned by calling them by name.

E386.4.p: Walking backward twelve times around a grave raises the ghost.

E386.5.p: A ghost is summoned simply by someone remarking aloud what they would do if one appeared. The careless words themselves bring the ghost.

E387.p: This heading lists the various motives for which people call a dead spirit back from the dead.

E387.1.p: A living person calls a ghost up in order to converse with it.

E387.1.1.p: Dead people are summoned out of their graves so that they can make a declaration or statement.

E387.2.p: A ghost is summoned so that the summoner can obtain something from it, such as an object or information.

E387.2.1.p: A son calls up the ghost of his dead father in order to retrieve the father's sword.

E387.3.p: A ghost is summoned through necromancy, the practice of magically raising the dead, typically to gain knowledge or power.

E389.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a ghost is summoned, covering cases that do not fit the more specific headings.

E389.1.p: A ghost can only be summoned by a king; if anyone else calls it, the ghost appears head downward.

E389.2.r: Jewish: Neuman. Cf. Shakespeare Hamlet (“ghost scene”).
E389.2.p: A summoned ghost can be seen and heard only by the person who summoned it, and no one else.

E390.p: Miscellaneous tales of a friendly return from the dead that do not fit the more specific headings under this section.

E401.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 63, Beal XXI 324; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 2 No. 20.
E401.p: Voices of the dead are heard coming from a graveyard.

E401.0.1.p: A ghostly voice is heard on a battlefield where the dead have fallen.

E402.r: E337.1, E236.7.) Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 24 Nos. 211—214; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 250; England: *Baughman.
E402.p: Mysterious noises that seem to come from ghosts are heard, such as singing, animal cries, or footsteps.

E402.1.p: Ghostly noises are heard that are made by the ghost of a particular person.

E402.1.1.p: A ghost of a human being is heard making vocal sounds, such as calls, moans, cries or screams.

E402.1.1.1.p: The ghost of a human being is heard calling out.

E402.1.1.2.p: The ghost of a human being is heard moaning.

E402.1.1.3.p: The ghost of a human being is heard crying out or screaming.

E402.1.1.4.p: The ghost of a person, unseen, is heard singing.

E402.1.1.5.p: The ghost of a person, unseen, is heard snoring.

E402.1.1.6.p: The ghost of a person, unseen, is heard sobbing or crying.

E402.1.2.p: Footsteps are heard, though the ghost walking them cannot be seen.

E402.1.3.p: An invisible ghost is heard playing a musical instrument.

E402.1.3.1.p: An invisible ghost is heard blowing a conch shell.

E402.1.4.p: An invisible ghost is heard rattling or jingling chains.

E402.1.5.p: An invisible ghost is heard rapping or knocking.

E402.1.6.p: A loud crash like breaking glass is heard, but no broken glass is found afterward.

E402.1.7.p: An invisible ghost is heard slamming a door.

E402.1.8.p: Various other sounds are made by the unseen ghost of a person.

E402.2.p: Animals that are dead but still heard as ghosts make sounds although unseen.

E402.2.1.p: The ghost of a rooster is heard crowing though it cannot be seen.

E402.2.2.p: The ghost of a donkey is heard braying though it cannot be seen.

E402.2.3.p: The ghost of a horse is heard as hoofbeats though it cannot be seen.

E402.3.p: A sound is made by some ghostly object that cannot be seen.

E402.4.p: Ghostly, otherworldly music is heard with no visible musician.

E410.r: (Cf. D2151.1.2.3.) Dead unable to rest in peace. Aside from the references given in the numbers immediately following, see E200—E399 passim. Jewish: *Neuman; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 48.
E410.p: A dead person who cannot rest in the grave comes back as a restless ghost.

E410.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 99.
E410.1.p: The ground shakes or rumbles when a ghost rises from its grave.

E410.2.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 99.
E410.2.p: A ghost shakes earth off itself when it rises from the grave.

E411.r: *Herbert III 380 No. 127; Alphabet Nos. 198, 300, 386, 701, 703, 752; Irish: Beal XXI 330, O’Suilleabhain 96; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 4 Nos. 31—34; Spanish Exempla: Keller; England, Wales: *Baughman; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 242; Africa (Fang): Trilles 134.
E411.p: The dead cannot find peace because of a sin they committed while alive, so they return as restless ghosts.

E411.0.1.p: A sinner's dead body is buried, but a hand sticks up out of the grave.

E411.0.2.p: A restless dead sinner is brought to a priest so that they can be forgiven and absolved.

E411.0.2.1.p: A dead sinner comes back from the grave to perform penance for their wrongs.

E411.0.2.2.p: A person who died without confessing their sins cannot rest in the grave.

E411.0.3.r: McKay Bealoideas III 141; Icelandic: *Boberg; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 113 No. 4; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 39 No. 4; Finnish-Swedish: cf. Wessman 1 Nos. 7—9; U.S.: *Baughman.
E411.0.3.p: A horse cannot pull the body of a wicked dead man away.

E411.0.3.1.p: The body of a dead wicked person cannot be moved from the place where it lies.

E411.0.4.p: A sinner's soul wanders in the space between earth and heaven, unable to go to either.

E411.0.5.p: The other dead drive a sinner out of the graveyard.

E411.0.5.1.p: A rich man is dragged out of his grave by demons, which happens because he was buried in consecrated ground, and is thrown into a grave in unblessed ground.

E411.0.6.r: (Cf. V62.1.) Loomis White Magic 44; Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3748; Danish: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
E411.0.6.p: The earth refuses to accept a buried body and pushes it back up.

E411.0.7.p: Demons throw an evil man out of his grave, and only his burial shroud remains in the ground.

E411.0.8.p: A saint's body moves by itself so that it lies properly north and south instead of northeast and southwest.

E411.1.r: *Type 760; Jellinek Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 323; Fb “gjenganger” I 443b, “lig” II 412b; Tobler 83, 90.—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 4 No. 32; England, U.S.: *Baughman; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 678; Greek: Aeschylus Eumenides 100.
E411.1.p: A person who committed murder cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.1.1.r: (Cf. E334.7, E431.16.) Fb “lys” II 481b, “selvmord” III 183b; Hartland Science 238; Tobler 22.—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 4 No. 35, 7 No. 53; Lithuanian: Balys Ghosts; England, U.S.: *Baughman.
E411.1.1.p: A person who killed themselves cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.1.1.1.p: Suicides must wander the earth until the time when they would have died naturally.

E411.2.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 228; English: Wells 61 (Awntyrs off Arthure at the Terne Wathelyne), Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
E411.2.p: A person who committed adultery cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.2.1.p: A priest's concubine cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.2.2.p: The devil's mistress keeps haunting the living after she dies.

E411.3.p: A person who swore a false oath cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.4.r: Herbert III 83; Alphabet Nos. 704, 784; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
E411.4.p: A usurer (someone who lends money at crushing interest) is denied peace after death and cannot rest in his grave, so his spirit walks.

E411.5.r: Fb “gjenganger” I 443b; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 47 No. 326A*; England: *Baughman.
E411.5.p: A swindler, a person who cheated others, cannot rest in his grave because of his fraud.

E411.6.p: A person who was never polite enough to say good morning cannot rest in the grave after death.

E411.7.p: A monk who dies without his cowl (hood or monastic habit) cannot rest in his grave and returns as a ghost.

E411.8.p: The spirit of Pontius Pilate appears from time to time on Mount Pilatus and keeps washing his hands.

E411.9.p: A magician who has sold his soul to the devil asks his servant to bury him properly, but when the coffin is lowered it bursts open.

E411.10.r: See all references to E334ff., especially E334.5, E411.1, E411.1.1, E413, E414. U.S.: Baughman.
E411.10.p: People who die a violent or accidental death cannot rest in their graves and come back as ghosts.

E412.p: A person who is under a religious ban or curse from the church cannot rest in the grave and walks as a ghost.

E412.1.p: A person who has been excommunicated (formally expelled from the church) cannot rest in the grave.

E412.2.r: *Fb “udøbt” III 960a; Tobler 47; Irish: Beal XXI 315, O’Suilleabhain 41; England: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3557.
E412.2.p: A person who was never baptized cannot rest in the grave.

E412.2.1.p: A person who was never christened cannot rest in the grave and also cannot enter heaven.

E412.2.2.p: The mother of an unbaptized child cannot rest in her grave.

E412.3.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 228ff.; Fb “spøgelse” III 521b; Ireland, U.S.: *Baughman; Greek: Fox 145; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 3 No. 25; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 123; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 342.
E412.3.p: A person who did not receive the proper funeral rites cannot rest and returns as a ghost.

E412.3.1.p: A dead man comes back as a ghost because he was buried without a cap on his head.

E412.3.2.p: A naked ghost asks a man for a shirt, and in return promises him good luck at the market.

E412.3.2.1.p: A ghost asks the living to wash his shirt for him.

E412.3.3.p: A dead man asks for shoes, because he was buried without them and so cannot rest.

E412.4.r: Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 2 No. 19; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3591.
E412.4.p: A child who has been cursed by his father cannot rest in the grave.

E412.5.p: The ghost of a person who desecrated (violated the holiness of) a church cannot rest.

E413.r: (See all references to E231, E334, E337.1.1, E337.3.) *Fb “spøgelse” III 521a, “gjenganger” I 443b; Jellinek Zs. f. Vksk. E413.p: A person who was murdered cannot rest in the grave and returns as a ghost.

E414.p: A person who drowned cannot rest in peace and returns as a ghost.

E414.1.p: A person who died by some other accident, not drowning, is likewise unable to rest in the grave and returns as a ghost.

E415.r: U.S.: Baughman (E354); North Carolina: Brown Collection I 679; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 245; West Indies: Flowers 430.
E415.p: A dead person cannot rest in the grave until a certain task has been completed.

E415.1.2.p: A dead person returns from the grave in order to reveal a treasure that was secretly buried.

E415.2.p: A dead rich man returns to scold his children, who have kept back money he had promised to the church.

E415.3.p: The ghost of a priest cannot rest because he failed to say certain masses for the dead.

E415.4.p: A dead person cannot rest until money he owed has been paid.

E416.r: (Cf. E345.1.) Kuhn Sagen aus Westfalen I 40f. No. 34, 118 No. 127, 177 No. 187; Sikes British Goblins (London, 1880) 149; Hoffman JAFL II 33; Frahm Am Urquell II 202; Kristensen Danske Sagn V (1897) 404ff., (1934) 308ff.
E416.p: A man who moved or removed boundary markers cannot rest in his grave.

E417.r: Madagascar: Sibree FLJ I 202ff., Larrouy RTP IV 305.
E417.p: A dead person speaks from the grave.

E419.p: Other kinds of dead people who cannot rest and wander, not covered by the preceding categories.

E419.2.p: The dead find no rest because someone knocks on the grave every day.

E419.3.p: The dead find no rest because grass is pulled up from the grave.

E419.4.p: The dead are disturbed and move when the cemetery is moved.

E419.5.p: The dead arise from their graves when someone plays the organ in church for the first time.

E419.6.p: Lovers who were buried apart are found in one grave every morning.

E419.7.p: A person who is missing a part of the body cannot rest in the grave.

E419.8.p: A ghost returns either to enforce its wishes about its burial or to protest that those wishes were ignored.

E419.9.p: A ghost moves back and forth between two graves, because people believe the body is in one of them.

E419.10.p: A ghost is troubled and cannot rest because of concern over the belongings it had in life.

E419.11.p: People who are buried with metal on them cannot rest peacefully in their graves.

E419.12.p: The ghosts of people who were eaten by tigers have a particular fate after death.

E420.p: The way a returned dead person, or ghost, shows itself to the living.

E421.p: A ghost that appears as a pale, insubstantial spirit rather than a solid body.

E421.1.p: A ghost that cannot be seen by ordinary people at all.

E421.1.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 243; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 64; N. A. Indian (Teton): Dorsey AA o.s. II (1889) 148.
E421.1.1.p: A ghost that only one person is able to see.

E431.p: Precautions taken at a funeral to keep the dead person from returning as a revenant.

E431.0.1.p: A test used to find out whether demons have entered a corpse.

E431.1.p: The burial service is read into a hat so the dead cannot walk again.

E431.2.p: Water is thrown on the corpse so that it will not return.

E431.3.p: Mould (earth or soil) is thrown on the corpse so that it will not return.

E431.4.r: Fb “gjenganger” I 444a; Frazer JAI XV 70; England, Scotland: *Baughman; Indonesia: Kruyt Het Animisme 264ff., Elshout De Kenja-Dejaks uit het Apo-Kajanggebied (Den Haag, 1926) 62.
E431.4.p: The coffin is carried out through a hole broken in the wall so the dead cannot find the way back.

E431.5.r: Von Trauwitz-Hellweg Urmensch und Totenglaube. 134ff.; Meyer Germanen 102; Wimberly 254; England: *Baughman; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis I 15f.
E431.5.p: The limbs of the dead are tied or chained so they cannot walk back.

E431.6.p: A piece of turf is laid on the chest of the dead to keep them from coming back.

E431.7.r: *Fb “hoved” I 655b; England: Baughman; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 252.

E431.7.2.p: The dead man is cut to pieces or beheaded again so that he will not return.

E431.7.2.1.p: The head is separated from the body by walking between them, so the dead man will not return.

E431.8.p: A dog is buried alive with the dead so that the ghosts will not walk.

E431.16.2.p: The body of a suicide is buried with a stake driven through the heart or body so it cannot walk.

E431.16.3.p: The body of a suicide is buried at a crossroads so that it will not walk.

E431.17.p: Criminals are buried at a crossroads so that they will not walk as ghosts.

E431.18.p: The body is cut up and its parts are buried in vessels or put in a bag so that the dead cannot return.

E431.19.p: The corpse is buried at midnight so that the dead person will not walk.

E431.20.p: The coffin is bound with an iron band so the corpse cannot return as a tiger.

E501.1.7.p: A famous historical or legendary hero is said to lead the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.7.1.p: King Herla is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.7.2.r: *Heilberg Dania IX 239, Nyrop ibid. X 177; BP IV 140; Oesterley No. 190.
E501.1.7.2.p: Theodoric is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.7.3.p: Wild Edric is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.8.r: Favorites are Herodias, Diana, Frau Holle.—Plischke 47; Schwartz Zs. f. Vksk. VII 231.
E501.1.8.p: A woman is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.8.1.r: Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXII (1912) 238 n. 7; Germania XVI (1871) 217; Dunlop-Liebrecht 474 n. 170; Grimm Deutsche Mythologie 599; La Tradition IV 69; *Kloss MLN XXIII 82; *Grunwald Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXX—XXXI 317.
E501.1.8.1.p: Herodias is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.8.2.p: Artemis is said to be the leader of the Wild Hunt.

E501.1.8.3.p: Hecate, the goddess of witchcraft, is the one who leads the spectral Wild Hunt of the dead riding through the night. A woman, rather than a man, is the leader of the ghostly hunting party.

E501.2.p: This heading covers the kinds of people and beings who are found riding in the Wild Hunt, the phantom hunting party seen in the night sky or woods.

E501.2.1.p: Knights, or armed noble horsemen, are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.2.p: Noblewomen or ladies are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.3.p: Witches are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.4.p: Courtesans, or women who were paid lovers of wealthy men, are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.5.p: Churchmen, such as priests and clergy, are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.6.p: Soldiers are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.2.7.p: Children who died without baptism are among the spirits who ride in the Wild Hunt.

E501.3.p: Members of the Wild Hunt are condemned to wander as ghosts because of sins they committed in life.

E501.3.1.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt as punishment for cruelty he showed in life.

E501.3.2.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he took his own life.

E501.3.3.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he killed his father.

E501.3.4.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he died without confession or absolution from a priest.

E501.3.5.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he failed to keep a required fast day.

E501.3.6.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he hunted on Sunday.

E501.3.7.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he wanted to keep hunting after he died.

E501.3.8.p: A huntsman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because he disrupted a church service.

E501.3.9.p: Wild huntsmen cannot die or find rest until the evil in the world is set right and things return to how they were before.

E501.3.10.p: A huntswoman is doomed to wander with the Wild Hunt because she murdered her own daughter.

E501.4.p: Animals accompany the wild huntsman, a phantom hunter who rides across the sky or land with a spectral pack and mounts.

E501.4.0.1.p: The animals in the wild hunt are the reborn spirits of people who were murdered.

E501.4.1.r: Schweda 25; England: Baughman; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 50f., 56, Beal XXI 318f.
E501.4.1.p: The phantom hunt includes dogs running with the wild huntsman.

E501.4.1.1.p: The wild hunt's pack of dogs is so huge that its sheer mass overwhelms and crushes people in its path.

E501.4.1.2.r: Schweda 25; *Schwartz Zs. f. Vksk. VII 232; Fb “Odins jæger” II 732a; England: Baughman.
E501.4.1.2.p: The hounds of the wild hunt have tongues that are on fire.

E501.4.1.3.p: The wild hunt's dogs have glowing, fiery eyes.

E501.4.1.4.p: The dogs of the wild hunt have eyes that hang out over their mouths.

E501.4.1.5.p: The dogs in the wild hunt are black.

E501.4.1.6.r: *Zingerle Sagen aus Tirol 590; H. Usener Dreiheit (Rheinisches Museum f. Philologie N. F. LVIII (1903) 1ff., 161ff.).
E501.4.1.6.p: Some dogs in the wild hunt have only three legs.

E501.4.1.7.p: The dogs of the wild hunt have wings.

E501.4.1.8.p: The dogs of the wild hunt run in a single line, one behind another.

E501.4.1.9.p: The dogs of the wild hunt are held on leashes by the huntsman.

E501.4.1.10.p: The dogs of the wild hunt bay loudly as they chase.

E501.4.2.p: The wild huntsman himself rides a horse, which has its own distinctive features.

E501.4.2.1.p: The wild huntsman rides a white horse.

E501.4.2.2.p: The wild huntsman rides a black horse.

E501.4.2.3.p: The wild huntsman rides a brown horse.

E501.4.2.4.r: Schweda 25; Schwartz Zs. f. Vksk. VII 235.
E501.4.2.4.p: The wild hunt's horse breathes fire from its nostrils or mouth.

E501.4.2.5.p: The wild huntsman's horse has glowing, fiery eyes.

E501.4.2.6.p: The wild huntsman's horse has only two legs.

E501.4.2.7.p: The wild huntsman's phantom horse has no head. It is one of the spectral animals that accompany the ghostly hunt.

E501.4.3.p: A female wild boar (sow) appears among the animals that follow the ghostly huntsman's pack.

E501.4.3.1.p: The sow accompanying the ghostly wild hunt has only one eye.

E501.4.3.2.p: The wild boar accompanying the ghostly wild hunt is blind.

E501.4.4.p: Two ravens fly along behind the ghostly wild huntsman as his companions.

E501.4.5.p: An owl, which is the ghost of a nun, is among the creatures that follow the wild hunt.

E501.5.p: Someone or something the spectral wild hunt chases. The hunters pursue a particular kind of victim.

E501.5.1.r: Plischke 65; Fb “Odins jæger” II 732b; Schwartz Zs. f. Vksk. VII 233.
E501.5.1.p: The wild hunter chases a woman.

E501.5.1.1.p: The wild hunter chases a naked woman and rides her down, cutting her in two.

E501.5.1.2.p: Prostitutes are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.1.3.p: Witches are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.2.p: Fairies are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.3.p: Wood-spirits are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.4.p: Unbaptized children are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.5.p: Animals are chased by the ghostly wild hunt.

E501.5.5.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt chases a hare.

E501.5.5.2.r: Schwartz Zs. f. Vksk. VII 232; RTP XXII 466.
E501.5.5.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt chases a deer.

E501.6.p: A ghostly figure appears beforehand to warn that the wild hunt is approaching.

E501.7.p: The wild huntsmen are seen in person, appearing as individual ghostly figures.

E501.7.1.p: The wild huntsmen have no heads.

E501.7.2.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have deer's heads on their bodies instead of human heads.

E501.7.3.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have their heads turned around backward on their necks.

E501.7.4.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt carry a skull tucked under their arms.

E501.7.5.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have their entrails hanging out of their open bodies.

E501.7.6.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt glow with light.

E501.7.6.1.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt breathe out fire.

E501.7.6.2.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have eyes that burn like fire.

E501.7.6.3.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt leave burning tracks behind them.

E501.7.6.4.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt are surrounded by fire.

E501.7.7.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have long hair.

E501.8.p: Describes the clothing worn by the wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt.

E501.8.1.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt wear black clothing.

E501.8.2.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt wear red clothing.

E501.8.3.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt wear white clothing.

E501.8.4.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt wear clothing of an old, bygone style.

E501.8.5.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt have their clothing belted and tied up tightly.

E501.8.6.p: One wild huntsman wears a black fur cap and carries a white staff.

E501.9.p: The wild huntsmen of the phantom hunt cannot be seen.

E501.10.p: Certain objects are said to accompany or form part of the phantom wild hunt.

E501.10.1.p: An empty shoe follows the phantom wild hunt.

E501.10.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt is led by a worn-out broom. The broom is one of the objects that accompany the spectral hunting troop.

E501.10.3.p: A wagon travels along with the ghostly wild hunt as part of the spectral procession.

E501.11.p: This heading covers the times when the ghostly wild hunt appears.

E501.11.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears during the night.

E501.11.1.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears at midnight.

E501.11.1.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt rides about at night until the cock crows at dawn.

E501.11.1.3.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears on St. John's Night, the night of the midsummer feast.

E501.11.1.4.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears on nights when storms are blowing.

E501.11.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears at certain seasons of the year.

E501.11.2.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears in winter.

E501.11.2.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears in the period between Christmas and Twelfth Night.

E501.11.2.3.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears on church feast days.

E501.11.3.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears at regular intervals.

E501.11.3.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears once every seven years.

E501.11.3.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears every year at the same moment.

E501.12.p: This heading covers the places where the ghostly wild hunt appears.

E501.12.1.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears in the woods.

E501.12.2.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears in a churchyard, the graveyard around a church.

E501.12.3.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears at a crossroads where roads meet.

E501.12.4.r: Schweda 13; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 678.
E501.12.4.p: The ghostly wild hunt appears beside a lake, river, or other body of water.

E501.12.5.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing near a hill or mountain.

E501.12.6.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing in a field.

E501.12.6.1.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing on an old battlefield.

E501.12.7.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing at a desert or barren place.

E501.12.8.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing at a castle.

E501.12.9.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing over a city.

E501.12.10.p: The spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party) is seen appearing at an old mill.

E501.13.p: Various signs or sounds that announce the coming of the spectral Wild Hunt (a phantom riding party).

E501.13.1.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by some loud noise.

E501.13.1.1.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by a loud explosion or blast.

E501.13.1.2.r: Schweda 20; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 250.
E501.13.1.2.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the clanking or rattling of chains.

E501.13.1.3.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the clashing of swords.

E501.13.1.4.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the ringing of bells.

E501.13.2.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by music.

E501.13.3.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the noise of horses.

E501.13.3.1.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the stamping of horses' hooves.

E501.13.3.2.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the neighing of horses.

E501.13.4.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the baying of hounds.

E501.13.5.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by the shouts of huntsmen.

E501.13.6.p: The Wild Hunt is announced in advance by a storm.

E501.13.7.p: The wild hunt, a phantom procession of riders and hounds, is announced by fire appearing when it approaches.

E501.14.p: Describes the route or movements of the wild hunt, the phantom hunting party that rides through the sky.

E501.14.1.p: The wild hunt rushes through the air, chasing its quarry above the ground.

E501.14.1.1.p: The wild hunt flies so low in the air that it nearly touches the ground.

E501.14.2.p: The wild hunt rides off in one particular fixed direction.

E501.14.3.p: The wild hunt rides three times around a pond.

E501.14.4.p: The wild hunt rides several times around a hill.

E501.14.5.p: The wild hunt travels all the way around the entire earth.

E501.14.6.r: (Cf. E501.17.5.4.) Plischke 64; Fb “port” II 862b, “Odins jæger” II 732b.
E501.14.6.p: The wild hunt passes through houses when their front and back doors are lined up in a straight line.

E501.15.p: Describes how the members of the wild hunt, the phantom huntsmen, behave.

E501.15.1.p: The wild huntsman blows his horn.

E501.15.2.p: The wild huntsman has his horse beaten.

E501.15.3.p: The wild huntsman forces people to carry him on their backs.

E501.15.4.p: The wild huntsman pays someone with leaves or wood shavings that turn into gold.

E501.15.5.p: A living smith is required to repair a wagon belonging to the wild hunt.

E501.15.6.p: Describes how the wild huntsman's dogs behave.

E501.15.6.1.p: The wild huntsman asks a person to hold his dogs.

E501.15.6.2.p: The wild huntsman releases his dogs to attack whoever he meets.

E501.15.6.3.p: The bite of the wild huntsman's dogs drives other dogs mad.

E501.15.6.4.p: The wild huntsman's dogs cannot cross a grave unless they are lifted over it.

E501.15.6.5.p: A ghostly huntsman's hound cannot be pulled out of a house it has gone into. It stays put no matter how hard people try to remove it.

E501.15.6.6.p: The dogs of the phantom huntsman eat dough, bread, meal and similar food. This shows they are ghostly creatures that take ordinary food.

E501.15.6.7.p: If someone grabs the wild huntsman's dog, it turns into a stick or a lump of black coal in their hands. The ghostly animal is revealed as an ordinary object.

E501.15.7.p: The phantom huntsman stops to water his horse. This is one of the ordinary things the ghostly hunter is said to do.

E501.15.8.p: The phantom huntsman is said to live in a room in a farmhouse. He is treated as a resident of the farm.

E501.16.p: Describes the strange events that happen when the wild hunt vanishes. These are the signs that accompany its departure.

E501.16.1.p: The wild hunt vanishes with a loud noise. The sudden bang or roar marks its departure.

E501.16.2.p: The wild hunt vanishes as the tops of the trees move. The treetops sway or shake as it departs.

E501.16.3.p: The wild hunt vanishes in a sudden gust of wind. A blast of wind marks its departure.

E501.16.4.p: The wild hunt vanishes in a column of fire. It disappears in a pillar of flame.

E501.16.5.p: The wild hunt vanishes in the middle of a storm. Its departure happens during bad weather.

E501.17.p: Ways of escaping or fighting the wild hunt. People use these methods to avoid being carried off or harmed by it.

E501.17.1.p: Certain people are beyond the power of the wild hunt and cannot be harmed by it. The hunt has no effect on them.

E501.17.1.1.p: The wild hunt has no power over herdsmen. Shepherds and cattle keepers are safe from it.

E501.17.1.2.p: The wild hunt has no power over churchmen. Priests and other clergy are safe from it.

E501.17.2.p: The wild hunt loses its power when it is beyond a certain distance. Being far enough away keeps a person safe.

E501.17.3.p: The wild hunt has no power at a crossroads. Standing at a crossing keeps a person safe from it.

E501.17.4.p: The wild hunt's power is avoided or escaped in some way. This is a general heading for the methods used.

E501.17.4.1.p: A person escapes the power of the wild hunt by praying. Prayer protects them from it.

E501.17.4.2.p: A person escapes the power of the wild hunt by using a set formula or magic words. The right words protect them.

E501.17.4.3.p: The power of the wild hunt, a ghostly chase of spectral riders, is escaped by offering a sacrifice to the huntsman's dogs.

E501.17.4.4.p: The power of the wild hunt, a ghostly chase of spectral riders, is escaped by staying silent.

E501.17.5.p: A person avoids being caught up with the wild hunt, a ghostly chase of spectral riders, by taking some protective action.

E501.17.5.1.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by keeping to their path, sometimes walking in the middle of the road or on its right side.

E501.17.5.2.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by moving out of the path the hunt is taking.

E501.17.5.3.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by staying indoors in a house with the windows shut.

E501.17.5.4.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by throwing themselves flat on the ground as it passes.

E501.17.5.5.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by remaining inside a drawn circle.

E501.17.5.6.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by holding a piece of bread.

E501.17.5.7.p: A person avoids the wild hunt by holding a particular plant.

E501.17.5.8.p: A person avoids hearing the sound of the wild hunt by pushing their fingers into their ears.

E501.17.6.p: The wild huntsman, leader of the ghostly chase, is calmed and stopped from troubling people.

E501.17.6.1.p: The wild huntsman is calmed by being given a sacrifice.

E501.17.6.2.p: The wild huntsman is calmed by being offered food.

E501.17.7.p: The wild huntsman, condemned to wander, is released from his restless wandering.

E501.17.7.1.p: The wild huntsman is released from wandering by a mould taken from Christ's grave.

E501.17.8.p: The wild hunt is compelled to leave the place where it is.

E501.17.8.1.p: The wild hunt is frightened away by being scolded.

E501.18.p: Meeting the wild hunt, a ghostly chase of spectral riders, has harmful consequences for the person who meets it.

E501.18.1.p: The wild hunt harms certain people who meet it, while others are not affected.

E501.18.1.1.p: The Wild Hunt, a phantom hunting party, harms people who mock it.

E501.18.1.2.p: The Wild Hunt, a phantom hunting party, harms thieves.

E501.18.1.3.p: The Wild Hunt, a phantom hunting party, harms people who are curious about it.

E501.18.1.3.1.p: When a man asks the Wild Hunt for some of its game, it throws him down his dead child.

E501.18.2.p: The Wild Hunt throws human flesh at anyone who sees it, and this harm cannot be undone.

E501.18.3.p: The Wild Hunt throws horses' feet at anyone who sees it, and this harm cannot be undone.

E501.18.4.p: The Wild Hunt seizes a person and carries them away.

E501.18.5.p: The Wild Hunt knocks a person to the ground.

E501.18.6.p: Seeing the Wild Hunt drives a person insane.

E501.18.7.p: Seeing the Wild Hunt makes a person blind.

E501.18.8.p: Seeing the Wild Hunt causes the head to swell.

E501.18.9.p: Seeing the Wild Hunt causes a person to stick an axe or knife into their own foot.

E501.18.10.p: Seeing the Wild Hunt causes death.

E501.19.p: Ways to undo the harm caused by seeing the Wild Hunt.

E501.19.1.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by seeing it again a year later at the same place.

E501.19.2.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by asking the huntsmen for salt.

E501.19.3.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by asking the huntsmen for parsley.

E501.19.4.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by asking to share in its booty, which is the same kind of flesh it has already thrown down.

E501.19.5.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by eating some of the flesh it threw down.

E501.19.6.p: The harm from seeing the Wild Hunt is undone by prayer.

E501.20.p: A wild hunt, a phantom procession of riders and hounds sweeping through the sky, is seen as a sign of coming events.

E501.20.1.p: The sight of a wild hunt warns that disaster is coming.

E501.20.1.1.p: The sight of a wild hunt warns that war is coming.

E501.20.1.2.p: The sight of a wild hunt warns that a plague or epidemic is coming.

E501.20.2.p: The sight of a wild hunt signals that the coming year will bring a good harvest or plenty.

E501.20.3.p: The wild hunt is taken as a sign of what the weather will do.

E502.r: *Schweda 59ff.; *Hartland Science 216ff.; Howey 9; Irish myth: *Cross; England, Scotland, Ireland, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
E502.p: Soldiers killed in battle rise from their resting place, such as a hill, grave, or grotto, and march about, or send their leader to do so.

E510.p: The ghosts of sailors or travelers who died at sea or on the road wander as phantoms.

E511.p: A wicked sea captain is condemned to sail his phantom ship forever and never reach harbor.

E511.1.p: The reason given for the Flying Dutchman's endless punishment.

E511.1.1.p: The Flying Dutchman is condemned to sail forever because he was cruel.

E511.1.2.p: The Flying Dutchman is condemned to sail forever because he made a pact with the Devil.

E511.1.3.p: The Flying Dutchman is condemned to sail forever because he defied a storm.

E511.2.p: Details about the Flying Dutchman's phantom ship itself.

E511.2.1.p: The crew of the Flying Dutchman's phantom ship are dead men.

E512.r: “Peter Rugg the Missing Man.” Boasts that he will reach home despite storm or never see his home again. He always travels in hard shower of rain or just ahead of one. U.S.: *Baughman.
E512.p: A phantom cart driver is doomed to wander because he spoke blasphemy.

E520.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Geist”; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 22 No. 201; New York: Jones JAFL LVII 243.
E520.p: Animals that return after death as ghosts.

E521.p: A ghost of a tame farm animal that returns to haunt.

E521.1.r: *Howey 31; *Fb “stud” III 619b, “hest” I 599b, “helhest” I 584b; *Kittredge Witchcraft 177 n. 31; *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 164ff.; England: Baughman.
E521.1.p: The ghost of a horse that returns after death.

E521.1.1.p: The ghost of a horse that appears without a head.

E521.1.2.r: Fb “helhest” I 584b; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 15, 420, 1011, III 1517.

E521.2.p: The spirit of a dead dog returning to the living world.

E521.2.2.p: The ghost of a dog that has no head.

E521.3.p: The spirit of a dead cat returning to haunt the living.

E521.4.p: The spirit of a dead calf, a young cow, returning as a ghost.

E521.5.p: The spirit of a dead hog, or pig, returning as a ghost.

E521.5.0.1.p: The ghost of a hog that has no head.

E521.5.1.p: The spirit of a dead female pig, a sow, returning as a ghost.

E522.p: The spirit of a dead wild animal returning as a ghost.

E522.1.p: The spirit of a dead fox returning as a ghost.

E522.2.p: The spirit of a dead bear returning as a ghost.

E523.p: The spirit of a dead fish returning as a ghost.

E524.p: The spirit of a dead bird returning as a ghost.

E524.1.p: The spirit of a dead goose returning as a ghost.

E524.2.p: The spirit of a dead rooster, or cock, returning as a ghost.

E530.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Geist”; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 23 No. 205.
E530.p: Inanimate objects that appear as ghosts or spirits after they have been destroyed or lost.

E530.1.r: Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 23 No. 210; England, Scotland, U.S.: *Baughman.
E530.1.p: Ghosts that appear as glowing or pale lights rather than as solid figures.

E530.1.1.p: A ghostly light follows behind a ghost, marking its presence as it moves.

E530.1.2.p: A ball of fire haunts the person who committed a murder, pursuing or troubling the killer.

E530.1.3.p: A ghostly light hovers over or haunts the spot where someone is buried.

E530.1.4.p: A ghostly light appearing on a farm warns that the people living there will soon have to move away.

E692.2.p: A mean person is punished after death by being reborn as a hyena.

E692.3.p: A tricky potter is punished after death by being reborn as a crab.

E697.p: A vulture eats only those who will be reborn as human beings in their next life.

E714.10.p: An ogre's soul is kept in a pale spot just below his right ear, and that spot must be found to kill him.

E714.11.p: A being's life or soul is kept inside its entrails, so harming its guts is what can kill it.

E714.12.p: A being's soul is kept in its hair, so cutting or harming the hair can kill or weaken it.

E715.1.1.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a duck, so the duck's safety determines the person's survival.

E715.1.2.p: A separated soul is hidden in the crop, or throat pouch, of a sparrow.

E715.1.3.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a parrot.

E715.1.3.2.p: An ogre keeps his life inside a parrot, and the ogre can speak from within the parrot.

E715.1.4.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a crane.

E715.1.5.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a starling.

E715.1.6.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a raven.

E715.2.r: (Cf. B175.) BP III 440; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
E715.2.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a fish, so the fish's fate determines the person's.

E715.3.p: A separated soul is hidden inside an insect.

E715.3.1.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a bee.

E715.3.2.p: A separated soul is hidden inside a fly.

E715.3.3.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a hornet. As long as the hornet lives, the person lives; if it is destroyed, the person dies.

E715.4.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a wild animal. The person's life depends on that animal staying safe.

E715.4.1.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a deer. Harming the deer harms or kills the person.

E715.4.2.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a wolf. The person's life depends on the wolf.

E715.4.3.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a walrus. The person's life depends on the walrus.

E715.4.4.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a seal. The person's life depends on the seal.

E715.5.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a snake. The person's life depends on the snake.

E715.5.1.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside a toad. The person's life depends on the toad.

E715.6.p: A person's soul is kept outside the body, hidden inside one of a hydra's heads. The hydra's life and the person's life are linked through that head.

E718.p: An ogre keeps several separate souls, hidden in different things: a tree, a fish, and a honey bee. Destroying all of them is needed to kill him.

E721.1.2.p: The soul of a sleeper is kept from returning to its body, so the sleeper does not wake or dies.

E721.1.2.1.p: The soul of a sleeper is kept from returning because it is trapped in animal form.

E721.3.p: Illness is caused by a soul that has wandered away from the body.

E721.4.p: A wandering soul is held captive or kept from returning by ghosts.

E721.5.p: A wandering soul takes on various shapes or forms.

E721.5.1.p: A wandering soul takes the shape of a wolf.

E722.1.2.p: At death the soul appears as a black or white being.

E722.2.4.p: The soul of a condemned person is forked out of the body by Satan.

E722.2.6.p: When someone dies, doors fly open by themselves.

E722.2.7.p: The soul weeps as it leaves the body.

E722.2.8.p: The soul is unwilling to leave the body at death.

E722.2.8.2.p: The soul hovers over the body, unwilling to part from it.

E722.2.9.p: Dead friends come to fetch the soul of a dying man.

E722.2.10.p: God or an angel takes the soul away at death.

E722.2.11.p: The soul leaves the body through the eye.

E722.2.12.p: The soul leaves the body because God kisses the person on the mouth.

E722.3.1.p: The soul cannot go far from the grave.

E722.3.1.1.p: The soul stays near the dead body.

E723.p: The general idea that a living person's wraith, or double, can separate from the body and act apart from it.

E723.3.p: A wraith stands in for a person who cannot perform a duty at the required time.

E723.4.p: A wraith does something that the living person wishes to do but cannot do while alive in the body.

E723.4.2.p: The wraith of a murderer tells the authorities where to find the girl he has killed, even though he himself is in church at the time.

E723.4.3.p: The wraith of a debtor, at the time of his death, tries to find the creditor he owed money to.

E723.4.5.p: A wraith brings news to someone that a member of the family has died.

E723.4.6.p: A wraith goes to check on the well-being of a person who is far away.

E723.6.p: A person's wraith appears to announce that the person has died.

E723.7.4.p: A wraith slams a gate shut.

E723.7.7.p: A wraith is seen riding a horse.

E723.8.p: A wraith appears as a warning that some disaster is about to happen.

E723.8.1.p: A wraith appears before a mine disaster, warning of it.
