E750.2.1.p: A dead person who lived a good life crosses a bridge to the otherworld without fear.

E750.2.2.p: The soul must pass through a dangerous valley on the way to, or in, the land of the dead.

E750.2.3.p: A tree with branching limbs serves as the road that souls travel.

E750.3.p: The soul makes its journey to the world of the dead riding a reindeer.

E750.4.p: The soul leaves its possessions behind along the road to its final resting place.

E751.r: Irish: *Cross; O’Suilleabhain 62, 78, Beal XXI 324, 327; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
E751.p: Souls are gathered and judged at the Day of Judgment at the end of the world.

E751.0.1.p: There will be two separate resurrections of the dead.

E751.1.r: (Cf. Q155.1.) Fb “veje” III 1025b; Irish myth: Cross.
E751.1.p: At Judgment Day, souls are weighed on a scale to determine their fate.

E751.2.p: Souls wait for Judgment Day in the form of birds.

E751.3.p: Irish souls will be judged on Judgment Day by Saint Patrick.

E751.4.p: On Judgment Day the dead are sorted into four (or five) groups.

E751.5.p: Sinners' souls must spend seven years under the sea before the end of the world.

E751.6.p: The resurrection of the dead will happen on a Sunday.

E751.7.p: Judgment Day will be on a Monday.

E752.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Arme Seelen”; Irish myth: *Cross.
E752.p: Souls that are lost, wandering or in danger of damnation.

E752.1.p: A soul is in danger of being lost once it has left the body.

E752.1.1.r: (Cf. G303.7.1.3.) French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 13; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 91 No. *773A.
E752.1.1.p: The devil, disguised as someone else, hunts down souls.

E752.1.2.p: Fiends toss a soul back and forth between them like a ball.

E752.1.2.1.p: Demons amuse themselves by tormenting souls in hell.

E752.1.3.r: Africa (Fang): Einstein 70ff., Trilles Bulletin de la Société Neuchâteloise de Géographie XVI 190ff.
E752.1.3.p: The souls of the dead are caught and held by someone or something as soon as they leave the body, so they are in danger of being lost.

E752.2.r: Frazer Golden Bough III 60; *Fb “djævel” IV 99b.—Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 464.
E752.2.p: A soul is carried off by a demon or the Devil, who takes it away to damnation.

E752.3.p: A raven carries off the souls of the damned.

E752.4.p: A lost soul appears in the form of raven feathers.

E752.5.p: Hell-hounds escort a soul down to the lower world, the place of the damned.

E752.6.p: A soul destined for hell is shown a glimpse of heaven.

E752.7.p: A lost soul is eaten away by worms.

E752.7.1.p: Abandoned souls survive by feeding on spiders and night moths.

E752.8.p: The souls of the dead are eaten by sky-spirits.

E752.9.p: The souls of the wicked are eaten by a deity.

E752.10.p: Precautions are taken with the corpse before burial so that evil spirits cannot enter it and use it.

E752.10.1.p: The corpse must be watched carefully until it is buried, so that no evil spirit can get into it.

E752.10.2.p: A light must be kept burning beside the corpse to keep evil spirits away.

E754.r: *Frazer Golden Bough III 55ff.; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 327.
E754.p: Souls that were in danger of being lost are saved.

E754.1.p: A soul condemned to hell is recovered and rescued.

E754.1.1.r: Alphabet No. 592; Wells 171 (The Gast of Gy); Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 331, O’Suilleabhain 98; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 89 No. 760C*, Keller; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 294 No. 7.
E754.1.1.p: A condemned soul is saved because someone prays for it.

E754.1.1.1.p: Demons have no power over souls that have been entrusted to God in prayer before sleep.

E754.1.2.r: (Cf. V250.) Crane Miraculis 84 No. 5, 86 No. 10, 87 No. 12, 93 No. 27; Ward II 605 No. 11, *607 No. 16, 635 No. 36, 670 No. 3, 672 No. 7; Wells 167 (Vernon Miracles).
E754.1.2.p: A condemned soul is saved through the intervention of the Virgin Mary.

E754.1.3.r: (Cf. Q520.) Alphabet No. 697; Irish myth: Cross.
E754.1.3.p: A condemned soul is saved through penance, or acts of atonement for its sins.

E754.1.4.p: A condemned soul is saved through the help of a holy person.

E754.1.5.p: A soul condemned to hell is freed when God chooses to release it.

E754.1.6.p: A condemned soul is released from hell through the intercession of Christ.

E754.1.7.p: A soul doomed to a bad afterlife is changed into one bound for Paradise because of a few grains of earth taken from a river bed.

E754.1.8.p: A condemned soul is released from punishment because the living weep for it.

E754.2.r: Fb “sjæl” III 213b; Wells 50, 175; Alphabet No. 316; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 307f., 322, O’Suilleabhain 24, 27, 99; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
E754.2.p: A soul that has been saved goes on to heaven.

E754.2.0.1.p: The souls of warriors are taken to Valhalla, the hall of the slain in Norse belief.

E754.2.1.p: Doves carry souls up to heaven.

E754.2.2.r: (Cf V232.2.) Hdwb. d. Märch. s.v. “Engel”; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
E754.2.2.p: Angels carry souls up to heaven.

E754.2.2.1.p: Angels of death are unable to bring a soul to heaven, so it does not get there by their hand.

E754.2.3.p: The dead and the living travel together to the gate of heaven.

E754.2.4.p: Dead children are invited to eat at God's table in heaven.

E754.3.p: Being buried in a particular ground guarantees that the soul goes to heaven.

E754.4.p: A hermit who starves himself to death for worldly fame would be damned, but his earlier good deeds save his soul.

E754.5.p: Souls are carried up to heaven in a chariot of light.

E754.6.p: Souls climb up pillars of smoke and light on their way to heaven.

E754.7.p: The souls of the pious become like angels.

E755.p: Where the soul ends up after death, such as heaven or hell.

E755.0.1.p: Boys who have been brought back to life choose to return to heaven.

E755.0.2.p: Angels sort souls, sending some to heaven and others to hell.

E755.0.3.p: The souls of the dead are presented to Adam.

E755.1.r: (Cf. A661.) K. Kohler Heaven and Hell in Comparative Religion (New York, 1923); Irish myth: Cross.
E755.1.p: Souls of the dead go to heaven, the place of reward for the good.

E755.1.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman. Maori: Clark 182.
E755.1.1.p: Heaven is arranged in ranks or levels, with different orders of souls or angels placed in order of rank.

E755.1.2.p: A river in heaven burns the wicked who wade into it while bringing joy and comfort to the righteous.

E755.1.3.p: Souls on their way to heaven travel through the Garden of Eden.

E755.1.4.p: Sixty thousand Jewish souls are said to be in heaven.

E755.2.r: A. Graf Miti, leggende et superstizioni del medio evo I 241ff.; K. Kohler Heaven and Hell in Comparative Religion (New York, 1923); Fb “helvede” I 589; Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 122, 281, 406; Alphabet No. 43; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 320, O’Suilleabhain 53; *Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
E755.2.p: Souls of the damned are sent to hell (Hades), the underworld of punishment.

E755.2.0.1.p: Souls held in hell are allowed to leave on Sundays.

E755.2.1.r: *Type 475; BP II 423, III 487; Köhler-Bolte I 69; Fb “potte” II 867a.
E755.2.1.p: Souls of people who drowned are punished in hell by being boiled in heated kettles.

E755.2.1.1.p: In hell, devils pull souls out of their bodies with hot pitchforks.

E755.2.2.p: Souls are kept in chains in hell.

E755.2.3.p: A lost soul must serve as a porter carrying loads in hell for seven years.

E755.2.4.p: Ghosts are forced to gather wood to fuel the fires of hell.

E755.2.4.1.p: The fires of hell are kindled in proportion to the sins of each sinner.

E755.2.5.p: Hell is a place of ice and extreme cold rather than fire.

E755.2.6.p: The dead are beaten with flails by demons.

E755.2.8.p: Christ speaks with the souls held in hell, in a conversation between them.

E755.3.r: **Landau Hölle und Fegefeuer in Volksglaube, Dichtung und Kirchenlehre (Heidelberg, 1909); Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 464, 467, 469, Crane Liber de Miraculis 86 No. 10; Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Fegefeuer”; Ward Catalogue of Romances II 440ff.; Herbert ibid. III 330; Alphabet Nos. 504, 661.—Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 330—333, O’Suilleabhain 95, 100, 102f.
E755.3.p: Souls go to purgatory, a temporary place where they are cleansed of sin before entering heaven.

E755.3.1.p: A soul in purgatory sends a letter asking his son to reward the person who prayed to free him from purgatory.

E755.4.p: Other places that souls of the dead are said to go to, not covered by the listed categories.

E755.4.1.r: Icelandic: De la Saussaye 298; Irish: Beal XXI 332.
E755.4.1.p: The souls of the dead are shut up inside a tree, where they are trapped rather than passing on.

E755.4.2.p: The soul of a dead person is kept or lodged inside a temple instead of going to its proper destination.

E756.p: A struggle breaks out between supernatural forces over who will get a person's soul after death.

E756.1.r: *Wesselski Märchen 199; *Fb “djævel” IV 99b; *Crane Miraculis 87 No. 11; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI No. 808*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *808; Estonian: Aarne in FFC XXV No. 808*; Jewish: *Neuman.
E756.1.p: Devils and angels compete with each other to claim a human being's soul.

E756.2.r: Fb “spille” III 487b; Irish: Beal XXI 329, O’Suilleabhain 90; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 52 No. 345.
E756.2.p: A person wins back their soul from the devil by beating him at a card game.

E756.3.r: Type 756B; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 157f., *249ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchen I 356a. s.v. “Busse des Räubers”; England, Wales: Baughman.
E756.3.p: A raven and a dove quarrel and fight over the soul of a man, the raven representing evil and the dove good.

E756.4.p: A saint takes a soul away from demons who have claimed it.

E756.4.1.p: A gambler's soul is won by a saint, who wins a dice game because the dice miraculously split to give the saint a higher score.

E756.5.p: A saved woman's soul helps her husband's soul fight off demons when he is attacked after death.

E757.p: A soul is shown praying to God or the saints.

E758.r: Type 802; BP III 274; Fb “rig” III 55a; Hdwb. d. Märch. I 351a s.v. “Burli im Himmel”.
E758.p: Heaven rejoices when a rich man arrives there, because it is so rare; a poor man enters without anyone noticing.

E759.p: Miscellaneous tales about the soul that do not fit the more specific headings under perils of the soul.

E759.1.p: A soul tries hard to make itself heard by the living, for example to send them a message.

E759.2.p: An angel tells a soul news or facts about a person still alive on earth.

E760.p: An object or animal is mystically linked to a person, so that changes to one reflect changes in the other, showing the person's condition.

E761.r: (Cf. E760.) Object (animal, person) has mystic connection with the life of a person, so that changes in the life-token indicate changes in the person, usually disaster or death. *Type 303; **Polivka The Life Tokens in Folk-Tales, Custom, and Belief (Národopisny Vestnik Ceskoslovansky XII [Prague, 1917]); *Chauvin V 87 No. 27 n. 1, V 295, VII 98 No. 375 n. 1; Penzer I 130, III 272 n. 1, X 210; Clouston Tales I 169ff.; Jacobs’ list s.v. “Life index”; *BP I 545, II 392; *Hartland Legend of Perseus II 1—54; **Nelson The Life-Index, a Hindu Fiction Motif (Studies in Honor of Maurice Bloomfield) 211ff.—Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “danger”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Oceanic (New Hebrides, Torres Straits, New Guinea, Indonesia): Dixon 133 n. 5; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 317 n. 149, *Hultkrantz 338—340, (California): Gayton and Newman 69; S. A. Indian (Quiché): Alexander Lat. Am. 173; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 81, (Basuto): Jacottet 212, 218 Nos. 31, 32.
E761.p: A person's life is linked to a token, such as an object, that reflects whether they are alive. Harm to the token signals harm to the person.

E761.1.p: Blood serves as a sign of a person's life: the blood's condition shows whether the person is alive or in trouble.

E761.1.1.r: (Cf. F961.3.1, V211.2.3.2.) Fb “vand” III 1000b.—England: Baughman; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
E761.1.1.p: Water turns to blood as a sign that the linked person is dying or in danger.

E761.1.2.p: A horn fills with blood as a sign of the linked person's life or death.

E761.1.3.p: A track or trail fills with blood as a sign of the linked person's life or death.

E761.1.3.1.r: Earth: dead by disease; water: drowned; blood: killed in battle. Icelandic: Boberg.
E761.1.3.1.p: Earth, water, or blood collects in a footprint as a sign of the linked person's life or death.

E761.1.4.p: A fish's blood, when spilled or shed, cries out to show that a person's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.5.p: A person's blood boils as a sign that their life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.5.1.p: The boiling blood stops boiling, showing that the person's life is no longer in danger or has been restored.

E761.1.6.r: Gaster Exempla 251 No. 373; Russian: Ralston Russian Folk-Tales 102.
E761.1.6.p: A person's blood changes color as a sign that their life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.7.p: A comb drips blood as a sign that its owner's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.7.1.p: A pair of gloves drips blood as a sign that the glove owner's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.7.2.r: Chauvin VII 198; Armenian: Macler Contes Arméniens 28.
E761.1.7.2.p: Scissors, a razor, or a knife drips blood as a sign that its owner's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.8.p: A piece of cloth turns bloody as a sign that the person connected to it is in danger or has died.

E761.1.9.p: A hero's horse is found standing in blood up to its knees in its stable, a sign that the hero's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.10.p: Milk turns bloody as a sign that a person's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.11.p: The roof spouts of a castle run with blood as a sign that a person's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.12.p: Meal ground in a mill comes out the color of blood as a sign that a person's life is in danger or has ended.

E761.1.13.p: A wound stops bleeding at the moment captives escape, showing that the person they were holding or bound has been freed or released.

E761.2.p: A staff or stick planted in the ground serves as a life token, showing by its behavior whether the person it stands for is alive.

E761.2.1.p: The staff stuck in the ground shakes as a sign that the person it stands for is in danger.

E761.2.2.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 8; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 220 No. 32.
E761.2.2.p: The staff stuck in the ground falls over as a sign that the person it stands for has died.

E761.3.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 1; Fb “lilie”; Böckel Psychologie der Volksdichtung 255; *Loomis White Magic 125f.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “flétrissement”; French: Sébillot France III 433; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 93, 96 n. 3, 97; Papua: Ker 61; Indonesian, Polynesian: Dixon 234 n. 46; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 87 No. 5, (Kaffir): Kidd 225, (Madagascar): Dandouau Contes Populaires de Sakalava 231.
E761.3.p: A tree or flower fades as a sign that the person connected to it is in danger or has died.

E761.3.1.p: Bamboo stalks grow with their joints upside down as a sign that the person connected to them is in danger or has died.

E761.3.1.1.p: Bananas ripen from the bottom up as a sign that the person connected to them is in danger or has died.

E761.3.2.p: Fruit rots on the tree as a sign that the person connected to the tree is in danger or has died.

E761.3.3.p: A tree's fruit falls to the ground as a sign that a particular person's life has ended. The fruit dropping is a token of death, showing the person's soul or life has gone out.

E761.3.4.p: Trees bow down or lie flat on the ground as a sign that a person's life has ended. The trees prostrating themselves serves as a life token showing the person has died.

E761.4.p: An object connected to a person darkens or rusts, and this change shows that the person's life is failing or has ended. It is a general life token of this kind.

E761.4.1.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 2; *Fb “kniv” II 221a.
E761.4.1.p: A knife stuck in a tree rusts, or becomes bloody, as a sign that the person linked to it is dying or dead.

E761.4.2.p: A picture of a person burns black as a sign that the person's life has ended.

E761.4.3.r: (Cf. D1163.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 5; Armenian: Macler contes Arméniens 28; Japanese: Ikeda.
E761.4.3.p: A mirror becomes black or misty as a sign that the person connected to it has died or is dying.

E761.4.4.r: English: Child I 201; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 4.
E761.4.4.p: A ring rusts as a sign that the person who gave or wears it is dying or dead.

E761.4.5.p: A silver object turns dark as a sign that the person linked to it has died or is failing.

E761.4.6.p: A charm dries up as a sign that the person who owns it is dying or dead.

E761.4.7.p: A sword rusts as a sign that the warrior or person linked to it is dying or dead.

E761.4.8.p: Beads stick together or cling as a sign that the person linked to them is dying or dead.

E761.4.9.p: Milk turns dark as a sign that the person linked to it is dying or has died.

E761.5.p: An object breaks or bursts as a sign that the person connected to it has died. This is a general life token of breaking.

E761.5.1.p: A pot breaks as a sign that the person linked to it has died.

E761.5.2.p: A zither string snaps as a sign that the person linked to the instrument has died.

E761.5.3.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 68f. n. 4; Fb “ring” III 60a.
E761.5.3.p: A ring springs apart or breaks open as a sign that the person linked to it has died.

E761.5.4.r: (Cf. D1171.6.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 7.
E761.5.4.p: A cup springs apart or breaks as a sign that the person linked to it has died.

E761.5.5.p: A stone breaks as a sign that the person linked to it has died.

E761.5.5.1.p: Stones bow down or lie flat on the ground as a sign that the person linked to them has died. This is a form of the stone-breaking token in which the stones prostrate themselves.

E761.5.6.p: Sheaves of grain bow down or lie flat as a sign that the person linked to them has died.

E761.6.p: A sign that a living person's life is in danger or has ended: a liquid becomes disturbed or changes in some way.

E761.6.1.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone No. 9; India: Thompson-Balys.
E761.6.1.p: A sign of a person's death or danger: water becomes troubled or stirred up.

E761.6.2.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 1; England: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
E761.6.2.p: A sign of a person's death: milk turns red.

E761.6.3.p: A sign of a person's death: a liquid begins to boil on its own.

E761.6.4.r: (Cf. D1045.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 69 n. 5.
E761.6.4.p: A sign of a person's death: beer foams up on its own.

E761.6.5.p: A sign of a person's death: wine sours into vinegar.

E761.6.6.p: A sign of a relative's death: milk churns or stirs agitatedly in a pan.

E761.7.p: A sign that a living person's life is ending, shown by a miscellaneous object, creature, or natural event.

E761.7.1.r: (Cf. D1076.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 6.
E761.7.1.p: A sign of a person's death: a ring tightens or presses on the finger of the person who wears it or of a relative.

E761.7.2.r: (Cf. D927.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 10.
E761.7.2.p: A sign of a person's death: a spring of water dries up.

E761.7.3.p: A sign of a person's death: leaves fall or drop from a tree.

E761.7.4.r: (Cf. E765.1.) *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 70 n. 11; Gaster Thespis 275ff.
E761.7.4.p: A sign of a person's death: a light, such as a lamp or fire, goes out.

E761.7.5.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 123.
E761.7.5.p: A sign of a person's death: dogs that were leashed begin pulling on their leashes.

E761.7.6.p: A sign of a hero's condition: a bird is sent each day to bring news, and if an owl comes instead, it announces the hero's death.

E761.7.7.r: Kirghiz: Radloff Proben der Volksliteratur der türkischen Stämme Südsiberiens III 85.
E761.7.7.p: A sign of a hero's death: bird feathers sink in a river.

E761.7.8.p: A sign of a person's death: a great wind blows.

E761.7.9.p: A sign of a person's death: a flaming shield goes out.

E761.7.10.p: A sign that an owner has been killed far away: his armor rattles at home.

E761.7.11.p: A sign that a person has died: a music box plays by itself while the owner waits for burial.

E761.7.12.p: A sign of a person's death: an arrow falls down.

E761.7.13.p: A life token: a sign such as a rice or paddy plant that stays healthy or withers, showing whether a person is still alive and thriving.

E761.7.14.p: A life token in which two rings swap places on girls' fingers, signalling the girls' fortunes or whether they still live.

E761.7.15.p: A life token: the direction a dagger points shows whether an ogress has been killed.

E765.p: A person's life is magically tied to some outside object or event, so that they die when that thing is destroyed or when it happens.

E765.1.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “vie”; Fb “lys” II 483ab; Gaster Thespis 275f.; Icelandic: *Boberg.
E765.1.p: A person's life is linked to a light or flame outside the body. When the light goes out, the life ends.

E765.1.1.r: *Krappe in Penzer Ocean of Story VIII 107; Anderson Die Meleagrossage bei den Letten (Philologus N. F. XXXIII [1923]); Icelandic: De la Saussaye 315, *Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 82 No. 708*A.
E765.1.1.p: A person's life is bound to a candle, and when the candle goes out the person dies.

E765.1.2.r: Hartland Science 205 (Olger the Dane); Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 65 n. 5 (Meleager).
E765.1.2.p: A person's life is bound to a burning brand or torch, and the person dies when it goes out.

E765.1.3.p: Each person's life is linked to a light in the lower world, and when that light is extinguished the person dies.

E765.2.r: *Krappe in Penzer Ocean of Story VIII 107; Irish myth: *Cross (Diarmaid); Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 5; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Hultkrantz 364—374.
E765.2.p: A person's life is bound to an animal's, so they live exactly as long as the animal does.

E765.3.r: *Krappe in Penzer Ocean of Story VIII 107; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Hultkrantz 364.
E765.3.p: A person's life is bound to some object, so that their life depends on its condition.

E765.3.0.1.p: A person's life is bound to a magic object; if that object is lost, the person dies.

E765.3.1.p: A person will live as long as a church stands, and dies when it falls.

E765.3.2.p: A girl's life is bound to a calabash plant, so that as the calabash grows, she grows.

E765.3.3.p: A person's life is bound to a tree, so that the tree's condition reflects their life.

E765.3.4.p: A girl lives only until her cowslip (a flower) is pulled up.

E765.3.5.p: A man's magic charm or object holds his life essence, so his life depends on keeping it safe.

E765.4.p: A person's death is tied to a certain future event, and they will die when that event happens.

E765.4.1.r: (Cf. E765.4.3.) Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 187.
E765.4.1.p: A father is fated to die when his daughter marries.

E765.4.2.p: A mother is fated to die when her daughter is courted or wooed.

E765.4.3.p: A father is fated to die when his daughter gives birth to a son.

E765.4.3.1.p: A father, and also the mother, will die on the same day as their daughter, under the rule that the father dies when she bears a son.

E765.4.4.p: A person's death is fated to come in the same year as their marriage.

E765.4.5.p: A person's death is tied to drinking from a particular horn; if they drink from it, they die.

E765.4.6.p: A snake cannot die unless it gives up the treasure it has hoarded.

E765.4.7.p: A man dies when a tortoise shell buried in the ground is dug up.

E765.5.p: One person's life depends on another person's life, so that when one dies or is harmed, the other is affected.

E766.p: An object dies or stops working at the moment its owner dies.

E766.1.p: A clock stops at the exact moment its owner dies.

E766.2.p: A tree dies when its owner dies.

E766.3.p: A post falls when its owners lose their estate.

E767.p: A person and an object have a mystical connection, so that what happens to one happens to the other.

E767.1.p: An ash pole repeatedly appears at a doorway on the day the owner's daughter dies; it is later used for coffin rests, having mysteriously escaped being used for other purposes.

E767.2.p: The clothes of a wicked person burn up when the owner dies.

E770.p: Vital objects: objects that have life inside them, so that harming or preserving them affects a person.

E771.p: A ring that contains a life, so that the life of its owner or another is bound to it.

E772.p: A sickle that contains a life, so that the life of a person is bound to it.

E780.r: (Cf. F1096.) India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 346 n. 246b.
E780.p: Vital body parts: parts of the body that keep living on their own, independent of the rest of the body.

E780.1.p: A detached vital body part attacks and kills enemies that attack its owner.

E780.2.r: (Cf. E781, E782.) Type 660; Haiti: Parsons MAFLS XVII (1) 59—62.
E780.2.p: When an animal's body part is transferred to a person or another animal, it keeps the animal's powers and habits.

E781.r: “Eyes exchanged”; Fb “øje” III 1166a; Köhler-Bolte I 434ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Gaster Thespis 333f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 139 No. 13.
E781.p: Eyes are successfully replaced, so that a person regains sight after losing their eyes.

E781.1.r: (Cf. F512.1.4.) *Type 660; BP II 552; Irish myth: Cross; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 299 n. 94.
E781.1.p: Lost eyes are replaced with the eyes of another person or an animal.

E781.1.1.p: A prince regains his sight after eyes stolen from water maidens are used to replace his own eyes. Eyes taken from another being are fitted in place of the lost ones and work again.

E781.2.r: *Type 533; *BP II 278 n. 1; *Köhler-Bolte I 463; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 83 No. 711A*; Missouri French: Carrière.
E781.2.p: Someone buys back lost eyes and has them put back in place, restoring their sight.

E781.3.p: Someone's eyes are borrowed by an animal, and the eyes are then returned to their owner and work again.

E782.p: A person has a lost or injured limb replaced, and the replacement works properly.

E782.0.1.p: A man borrows various limbs from others and successfully uses them as his own.

E782.1.r: *Type 706; *BP I 295; Fb “hånd” I 765b; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller, Nouvelles de Sens No. 12; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 2; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
E782.1.p: A lost or injured hand is restored to its owner, so that it works again.

E782.1.1.p: A man exchanges his hand for another person's hand, and the new hand works for him.

E782.2.p: Ribs are replaced with substitutes, specifically ribs taken from a chariot.

E782.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bras”.
E782.3.p: A lost or injured arm is restored to its owner so that it works again.

E782.3.1.p: An injured arm is replaced by another arm, which then works for its owner.

E782.4.r: *Type 753; *BP III 198; *Lowes Romanic Review V 368; Saintyves Saints Successeurs 248—251; Köhler-Bolte I 132, 297 n. 1; Dh II 169; Hoefler Zs. f. Vksk. I 304; Ons Volksleven III 43, V 28, 136f.
E782.4.p: A horse's leg is cut off and then replaced with another leg.

E782.4.1.p: An injured leg is replaced by another leg, which then works properly.

E782.4.2.r: Africa (Somali): Kirk A Grammar of the Somali Language (Cambridge [Eng.], 1905) 162f., (Ishhak): Kirk FL XV 391ff. No. 3, (Saho): Reinisch Die Saho-Sprache I 76ff. No. 3.
E782.4.2.p: A severed leg or legs grow back on their own.

E782.5.p: A tongue is cut out or lost and replaced with a substitute that works.

E783.r: (Cf. D992, F511.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 432.
E783.p: A head that remains alive even after being cut off from the body.

E783.1.r: *Kittredge Gawain 147ff.; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 61, *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Quiché): Alexander Lat. Am. 175; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 113 No. 8, (Bushman): Bleek and Lloyd 10.
E783.1.p: A head is cut off and then successfully put back on the body, restoring life.

E783.2.p: A severed head grows back again on the body.

E783.2.1.p: The winged horse Pegasus comes into being from the neck of the slain Medusa after her head is cut off.

E783.3.p: A severed head changes color, turning red and then white.

E783.4.p: A severed head opens its eyes.

E783.5.p: A severed head is still alive and can speak.

E783.6.p: A headless body is still alive and keeps functioning.

E783.7.p: A man continues to live for four (or seven) years after his head has been cut off.

E783.8.p: A dead, detached head thanks the person who buried it.

E784.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chair”; India: Thompson-Balys.
E784.p: A body part that has been cut off grows back again.

E785.p: A piece of skin stays alive after its owner has died.

E785.1.p: Skin from one body or animal is substituted for another's skin.

E785.1.1.p: A ewe's hide is grafted onto the skinless head of a wounded man.

E786.p: A heart is successfully replaced with another heart.

E787.p: An animal borrows or takes the stomach of another being.

E788.p: A woman's severed breast grows back once she gives birth to a child.

E789.p: Miscellaneous tales in which vital bodily parts of a being are involved in other ways.

E789.1.p: A being's internal organs are exchanged with those of an animal.

E790.p: Miscellaneous beliefs and tales about the soul.

E791.p: A man who forgets to count himself dies immediately afterward.
